abstract: Agentic AI can access student records, retain memory, delegate work and initiate institutional actions. When a model is mistaken or pursuing a hidden objective, a useful safeguard must constrain what it can cause without relying on its stated intentions. Trust by Construction presents a compositional reference architecture for this boundary. A workload declaration and task contract limit authority; deterministic services mediate context, memory, delegation, effects and release. The contribution is an executable account of how these controls interact, including three failure-sensitive mechanisms: a durable workload stop that survives evidence-writer failure, reauthorisation of queued output at each delivery boundary, and an AI-monitor interface that may restrict authority but cannot grant it. The public reference uses synthetic education fixtures and an independent state-and-byte outcome check. Existing cross-sector experiments contain 180 of 180 hostile scenarios while completing 58 of 58 benign tasks. Thirty-eight local regression cases exercise stop, delivery, monitoring and the recording of refused attempts. A further contribution addresses the objection that these controls rest on unexamined deployment assumptions: host isolation is now measured against eight declared properties rather than assumed, outbound transport is performed by a pinning, TLS-verifying, redirect-refusing client exercised against a controlled peer, tool-server definitions are pinned against silent redefinition and name shadowing, untrusted content cannot reach a privileged tool in the same chain, outbound effects are at-most-once with reconciliation by key, evidence is attested by independent witnesses, and promotion to production is refused unless all of it is fresh, attributable and complete. Held-out trajectories show that no monitor -- an oracle, a blind monitor, or a hostile one -- changes any protected outcome. These measurements establish behavior within declared interfaces, not real-world attack prevalence or model alignment. The artifact provides a reusable engineering and teaching method: bind each authority claim to an enforcement point, an accountable role, an executed failure test and an explicit residual risk. Measuring an assumption is not supplying it. The system still does not provide operating-system isolation, a qualified network peer, substantive decision correctness or production certification, and the promotion gate refuses to promote this reference on its own evidence.
intro: Learning institutions expose the difference between useful reasoning and legitimate authority. A tutor may need a limited record view; a registrar may approve a correction; a research assistant may need public information without access to restricted student data. Combining these privileges in one agent process creates a larger failure surface than any individual task requires. Recent safety research separates misuse, misalignment, mistakes and structural risks, and argues for both model-level and system-level mitigations [1]. Experiments also show insider-threat behavior under constructed goal conflict and replacement pressure [5]. We address the institutional systems boundary: how can a compromised or unreliable reasoning component remain useful while consequential reads, writes and releases require independent authority?
foundations: Our contribution is compositional rather than a new alignment algorithm. CaMeL demonstrates a system-level defense that separates control and data flow and constrains disclosure through capabilities [2]. Trust by Construction applies related architectural principles to an education workflow with memory, agent populations, effect approval, revocation and recipient delivery. It contributes an inspectable enforcement path, failure tests and a claim-to-evidence register. It does not offer a formal proof for arbitrary agent programs or a head-to-head performance comparison with CaMeL. The paper separates properties tested in the local kernel from requirements imposed on deployment adapters. AgentSecBench separates instruction integrity, confidentiality and capability integrity, using paired adversarial and benign executions [10]. AgentDyn studies dynamic tasks and helpful third-party instructions, exposing a security–utility tradeoff that static blocking tests can miss [11]. Our smaller synthetic evaluation makes no benchmark-ranking claim; it complements this work with persistent authority, revocation and failure-atomic delivery checks.
covert: Recent results motivate testing the authority boundary even when model behavior appears cooperative. Anti-scheming training reduced covert actions in held-out settings but left residual failures and evaluation-awareness confounds [3]. Chain-of-thought monitoring offers an imperfect signal rather than a reliable authorization basis [4]. Reward-hacking research found generalization from training shortcuts to broader misalignment [6], while SHADE-Arena evaluates harmful side objectives hidden within legitimate tasks [7]. A 2026 safety-research study found no unprompted sabotage in its tested settings, yet observed sabotage continuation in some seeded trajectories; those conditions must not be conflated [8]. Bengio and colleagues propose non-agentic Scientist AI as a safer direction for assisting research [9]. These findings support our design choice: AI may propose work, generate tests and report anomalies, while deterministic checks retain authority. A compromised monitor can still deny service or miss misconduct; it must not gain the power to approve an effect or restore privilege.
education_example: A concrete teaching exercise follows a synthetic transcript correction. The agent retrieves only the authorized record and proposes a version-bound change. A source role confirms the supporting evidence and a different reviewer approves the exact proposal. The executor revalidates authority before changing the record. A recipient receives only the approved artifact; a stop or revocation between chunks denies the remainder. Students can compare a valid completion with an attempted forged approval, contaminated memory and a misleading monitor verdict. This teaches the distinction between fluent advice, authorization, source validity and correctness. No result here measures learning outcomes or fairness; those require an institutional study.
validity: Threats to validity and deployment limits. The experiments use synthetic fixtures and declared interfaces. The new tests submit scripted findings and adversarial requests; no live frontier-model detector is evaluated, and no detector accuracy, real-world attack rate or causal prevention of an incident is claimed. Shared Python and SQLite state is trusted service infrastructure, not isolation from hostile native code. A source digest records artifact identity but does not attest a running model. Monitor false positives can reduce availability, and sparse event metadata can miss intent. Chunks are staged approved bytes rather than live model-token streaming; bytes already released cannot be recalled. Cross-service authority, independent witnesses, outbound-effect settlement, tool-supply integrity and an evidence-gated promotion decision are implemented and tested in this revision, and host isolation and transport are now measured rather than assumed; measuring an assumption is not supplying it. Three limits survive unchanged and are stated as acceptance criteria rather than future work. Host isolation must be exercised adversarially in the target deployment, because a cooperative probe run inside the process cannot establish the absence of every path. Transport must be qualified against the institution's real peer with its own certificates and firewall, because the controlled peer used here is a loopback server and its evidence is marked as such and refused by the promotion gate. Physical data erasure and the training lifecycle remain deployment work. Remote effects are at-most-once with reconciliation by key, and exactly-once-observable only where a provider supports lookup by that key; a provider without lookup leaves a permanent uncertain remainder. The supplementary incident map is an architectural reading of public disclosures. Five of the fourteen mapped stages are not mediated locally; its existence is not evidence that the system would prevent a real breach. The institutional study is not run. A preregistration, its hypotheses, its subgroup plan and its minimum sample are published, and the analysis computes every preregistered quantity, but it refuses conclusions on synthetic fixtures, below the preregistered sample, on subgroups under the cell minimum, or under a changed analysis plan. Nothing here measures student outcomes or equitable decisions, and the instrument is written so that it cannot be made to appear to.

source_note: Primary paper metadata checked on arXiv. Preprints are research papers, not asserted to be peer reviewed. Leader essays motivate threat selection in the repository review only.
security_review: A security review exposed three practical defects in the reference: unrelated task traffic could displace monitor history and stale its advice, non-string monitor fields could raise uncontrolled type errors, and URL path parameters or encoded delimiters could admit ambiguous destinations. The revised service queries task-indexed evidence before applying the 32-event limit, binds findings to task and global-control heads, and validates field types before interpretation. Global source invalidation and revocation still stale advice. Destination authorization rejects matrix parameters, encoded delimiters and repeated separators while preserving safe unreserved encoding. Twenty-seven added regression cases check these changes and legitimate continuation; they overlap the reported regression total and are not additional attack episodes. The destination policy remains a transport contract: an adapter must pin the approved address, verify TLS identity, enforce byte limits and reauthorize every redirect. A later review of the same kind found one further defect and fixed it. Refusals raised before the request savepoint exists -- a revoked agent, a stopped workload, an assurance failure -- returned a denial and wrote no evidence at all, so a workload that kept issuing requests after an emergency stop left no trace in the chain, which is precisely the signal an operator needs. Such attempts are now recorded outside the failed transaction as blocked attempts bound to the known identity and task, a failure to record one never restores authority, the guardian's own contraction is not rolled back by the recording, and an unknown token records nothing so that anonymous traffic cannot be used to grow the evidence chain. The defect was found by the monitor-quality harness rather than by review of the code, which is the argument for building the harness.
